Title: Three Attacks, Zero Exploits in Microsoft 365
Context: ClickFix and Session Hijacking In about eight minutes, an attacker gains access to an employee's inbox without installing any malware because the employee runs the malicious...
Full Text:
Most of us think of a breach as something technical, like an unpatched server or a zero day. We figure MFA makes a stolen password worthless. That thinking assumes the attacker breaks in using their own tools.

This blog breaks down three attacks that skip all of that. They work because an employee does something perfectly ordinary, like clicking a link or approving a login. The attacker gets in by abusing the victim's own tools and habits. We show how each one works so you can recognize the tradecraft before it's used against you.

ClickFix and Session Hijacking

In about eight minutes, an attacker gains access to an employee's inbox without installing any malware because the employee runs the malicious command themselves. It starts with a stolen login, the kind anyone can buy off the dark web for about the price of a large pizza. The attacker tries it, but MFA stops them at the door. Plenty of attacks would end there, but this attacker goes after the person who owns the password instead.

The bait is an email, and it takes almost no effort to write. The attacker asks ChatGPT for something that sounds like routine internal comms, like a company-wide note about an updated holiday policy. The attacker swaps in a link to a look-alike SharePoint site, adds a deadline, and tells people not to reply to their manager, because a quick check with the boss is how phishing gets caught.

The employee opens the email and clicks. The page shows a "prove you're not a robot" box. We've all done this countless times. But this time, clicking it discreetly loads a payload onto the employee's clipboard, and the page asks them to press the Windows key + R, paste, and hit Enter. That's ClickFix. The employee thinks they're finishing a verification, and they're running the attacker's PowerShell on their own machine.

Meanwhile, the PowerShell sends the attacker the employee's session cookies. The browser stores them when you tell it to keep you signed in, and most of us say yes so we don't have to log in over and over. The cookie carries the approved MFA. The attacker loads those cookies into their browser using a free extension called Cookie Editor, refreshes, and then lands in the employee's Outlook inbox. They have the password but never had the phone, and the stolen session makes that gap irrelevant. This is token impersonation, also called session hijacking, and it reaches well past Microsoft 365, since everything the browser held is up for grabs.

Over-Permissioned Apps and Global Admin

An attacker turns a standard user's phished login into a Global Admin account in under six minutes. This one starts with Standard Steve, who has an ordinary account and an ordinary workday. The attacker wants his access, so they put an Evilginx proxy between Steve and the login page, phish his credentials, and sign in as Steve. Steve hasn't set up MFA yet, so the attacker can register their own MFA, which means a password reset won't lock them out.

Steve can't open the admin center, but the Azure management portal and Entra are wide open, so the attacker starts looking around. In app registrations, they find something odd. Steve owns a finance integration app. Standard users don't usually own apps, and this one carries a directory-wide role management permission, which is about as powerful as permissions get. The attacker creates a new secret for the app with a two-year lifespan, so even if someone blocks Steve's account, the app still lets them in.

For the last step, the attacker describes what they want in plain English to n8n, a workflow automation tool, and asks it to make them a Global Admin. After a couple of minutes of back and forth, the workflow runs. Steve logs back in with the attacker's MFA and opens the admin center as a Global Admin. About seven controls could have stopped or slowed all of this, including keeping standard users out of the admin center and enforcing MFA registration.

Device Code Phishing

An employee signs in on Microsoft's real login page, and an attacker gets access to their mailbox without ever seeing the password. That's the attack behind EvilTokens, a phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platform that Huntress and Microsoft tracked hitting more than 300 organizations in about two weeks.

The attacker's part is small. They enter a company's domain into EvilTokens, and the platform creates a phishing email targeting that company's employees.

An employee opens a phishing email that has a short code in it, the type of code you get from Netflix. They go to the login page and sign in with the code like they would on any other day.

That sign-in is the moment the attacker gets in. The code is tied to the attacker's session, so when the employee signs in, access goes straight back to the attacker's back end. The employee used their own credentials and their own MFA on the real login page, and that's exactly what handed over the account. The attacker now has the employee's email and every document in OneDrive, and can search through it all.

The employee sees a normal sign-in and goes back to work while someone else reads their files. Because the attacker holds a live session, access can persist even after a password reset unless the session and tokens are revoked as well.

EvilTokens went from launch to takedown in under nine months. Microsoft's Principal Corporate Counsel Carlton Gammons, Huntress's Chief Legal Officer Lauren Zajac, and Product Manager Rich Mozeleski explain how Huntress's early research and a law written for the mob took it down.

The One Ordinary Action Every Attack Needed

Each attack asked the user for a single normal action, and each victim acted as a reasonable employee would on a busy day. That's why the defense has to start before the inbox.

For your users, that means knowing what these moments look like. A web page telling you to open the Run dialog is a ClickFix tell because no real CAPTCHA asks you to do that. A login code you never asked for deserves the same suspicion as a password prompt you didn't expect.

For admins, it means checking your tenant for the settings in the second attack, like who owns app registrations and which apps hold directory-wide permissions. Every one of those settings could have been closed.

If you only have time for one thing this week, pick one of those controls and check it in your own tenant.

Title: Huntress EU Data Hosting: What Phase 1 Means
Context: A first step: ingesting product data in the EU We've already kicked off our EU data hosting initiative, and we're halfway through Phase 1, which will continue through the end of...
Full Text:
For some organizations, EU data hosting is a requirement before they can choose a security partner. For others, it may not be required, but is strongly desired. Huntress has gained a significant number of partners and customers in Europe over the last three years, and we're incredibly grateful for their feedback on data hosting and how we can tailor our platform for their unique needs.

We're now actively working toward EU data hosting. But getting there will take time. It requires significant changes to how our platform is built and operated, so we'll move in phases and share more as the work progresses.

Our official EU Data Hosting statement lays out our official plans and serves as the source of truth as they evolve, but this post will cover the basics.

A first step: ingesting product data in the EU

We've already kicked off our EU data hosting initiative, and we're halfway through Phase 1, which will continue through the end of 2026. Here's what that means practically: for newly created accounts that select EU hosting, raw product data collected by supported Huntress products, along with backups, will be ingested and stored in a data center in Frankfurt, Germany. The products in scope are EDR, ESPM, SIEM, ITDR for Microsoft 365, and ISPM for Microsoft 365.

It's important to understand what this first step does and doesn't mean. Phase 1 brings ingestion and storage of raw product data into the EU, but not all processing. Huntress detection and investigation systems will continue to operate in the United States. Data needed for analysis—personal data such as usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, and hostnames—will be transferred to the US for processing. The results of that analysis—including detections (alerts), incident reports, and forensic evidence—will also remain in the US, along with account and billing data.

Phase 1 plan for Huntress EU data hosting

EU hosting will be selected at the account level, so all organizations within an account will use the same region. Existing customers who want EU hosting will need to create a second account. Data already stored in the US won't be moved to the EU during Phase 1.

The bottom line is that Phase 1 brings raw product data and backups into EU storage, while detection and investigation processing and their results remain in the US. We understand this still isn't ideal, which is why we're not stopping here.

What comes next

In Phase 2, we plan to move more of the work itself into the EU. Telemetry and forensic data, along with analysis results such as detections and investigations, would be processed and stored there. Some information would still remain in the US, including certain identifiers used to track and manage detections, as well as account, billing, and contact information. We're also evaluating options for migrating existing customers' historical data.

Phase 2 plan for Huntress EU data hosting

After Phase 2, we'll assess whether even more customer product and personal data should be brought into the EU. That longer-term work is less certain, and we'll define it as we make progress. We aren't committing to timelines for Phase 2 or beyond yet. We'll share more as plans develop.

It's important to note that Huntress will continue to operate a global Security Operations Center (SOC). Authorized team members outside the EU may access EU-hosted data when needed to support customers, respond to incidents, and help maintain the security and availability of our services.

Interested in testing?

If you're a partner or customer interested in taking part in Phase 1 testing, let your Huntress account manager know. We welcome your feedback as we work through this in stages.

For the complete scope and latest details, please refer to the official EU Data Hosting statement (if anything in this post differs from that statement, the statement takes precedence).

Title: Why Resilience Has to Come First
Context: Whether the disruption is a cyberattack or a technology failure, a business is only as resilient as its recovery plan
Full Text:
Acknowledgments: Special thanks to Bryson Byrd and Muhammad Yahya Patel for their contributions to this write-up.

Microsoft Outlook went down, US flights were grounded, and Chase banking customers reported problems accessing their accounts, all within a week. Even the National Security Agency's classified network, NSANet, was disrupted. Outages are dominating the headlines, and speculation is running wild. Tinfoil hats are having a moment.

Whether the disruption is a cyberattack or a technology failure, a business is only as resilient as its recovery plan. Here's what the outages show and what every business leader should be prioritizing.

The rush to find a culprit

When something this big breaks, people want a culprit. Bryson Byrd, Cybersecurity Advisor at Huntress, told The New York Times, in its coverage of the National Security Agency network disruption, that "you don't need a cyberattack to bring operations to a halt." He's also seen how quickly people label an outage a cyberattack or an AI failure before anyone has the details, which means decisions get made on conjecture.

What Microsoft, the FAA, and Chase say happened

Each organization pointed to a failure inside its own technology. A Microsoft executive said the outage, which began on November 12 and, according to ABC News, stretched across two workdays, stemmed from several problems piling up, including a hidden software flaw and reduced server capacity as demand rose. The FAA said its legacy equipment became unstable when data flooded its network, which disrupted communications and radar feeds. Chase cited a software bug in on-premises hardware systems and said customers kept access to their funds. The causes were different, but the problem for customers was the same.

Recovery isn't always a priority, but it should be

Muhammad Yahya Patel, Cybersecurity Advisor at Huntress, says spend has gone into preventing and detecting incidents, and far less into how the business keeps running when one gets through. The clearest sign is what happens when you ask leadership what the business does during an incident. You rarely get an answer that is both consistent across the room and detailed. Inconsistent answers show there's no shared plan, he says. Vague answers show nobody has practiced it. In a well-prepared organization, leaders can walk through the playbook without hesitation and know where the documentation is.

The business still has to keep running and recover, regardless of what caused the disruption. The test is whether its recovery plan has kept up with the systems it covers. A plan written only for cyberattacks leaves a gap, because a vendor outage like Microsoft's has no attacker to respond to.

Downtime is a business decision

Resilience is ongoing work that the board and executives own. It can't land on IT alone. Everyone should know their role in the recovery plan. An alternative system only helps if the business can switch to it.

Start by listing the services and technologies the business can't operate without. For each one, work out what downtime would cost in minutes, hours, days, and weeks. Then decide, service by service, whether to pay for an alternative to keep it running or accept that the business can go without it for a while. Accepting downtime is a legitimate decision. Discovering that you made it by default in the middle of an outage is the failure.

Where the plan is stored is part of the plan. If it's in SharePoint and an outage takes down Microsoft 365 or the network, you don't have a plan, so keep a copy offline. If a core service depends on one provider, decide how long you can go without it. Then check whether that provider has promised to restore it that fast. Any alternative has to be tested before it's needed, and every organization needs, at a minimum, a way to reach customers and partners outside its main systems.

Make recovery the priority

Ask your leadership team what the business does when systems go down. Compare the answers. If they differ, bring the group together to agree on the services the business can't function without. That list is where you start working out what downtime costs and which providers each service depends on.

The next outage may have a different cause, but customers will ask the same thing: can you keep running? The answer should be ready before they ask.

Title: Handling the NIST 800-171 Rev 3 Transition
Context: However, the current requirements for defense contractors, found in DFARS 252
Full Text:
The June 2026 proposed FAR CUI rule requires Revision 3 of NIST Special Publication 800-171 for contractors safeguarding Controlled Unclassified Information. However, the current requirements for defense contractors, found in DFARS 252.204-7012 and 252.204-7021, stipulate Revision 2. This creates a transition period between the two revisions, where defense contractors may need documentation for both revisions, until multi-year contracts with Rev 2 fade out.

What differs in Rev 3

Rev 3 is a restructured set of requirements, sourced from the federal catalog of security and privacy controls (NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5). Three major changes stand out:

More families. Rev 3 organizes requirements into 17 families, versus the 14 used in Rev 2. Planning, System and Services Acquisition, and Supply Chain Risk Management are new.

Merged and withdrawn requirements. Many Rev 2 requirements are folded into other Rev 3 requirements, forming structured lists instead of single-sentence requirements.

Organization-defined parameters. Rev 3 leaves blank variables, such as event types, frequencies, and time periods, to be defined by you or a government customer.

The overall effect is larger, more detailed requirements with more assessment objectives, leading to more documentation that forms more complete processes.

The four-step transition

The good news is that moving from Rev 2 to Rev 3 does not mean starting over. If we walk through the steps to transition an organization from Revision 2 to Revision 3, we can see how this works.

Step 1: Relocate Rev 2 requirements

Rev 3 uses an expanded format. A Rev 2 requirement often becomes a list item inside a different Rev 3 requirement. Build a map from each Rev 2 objective to its new home before anything else.

Rev 2 spread the topic of malicious code protection across three requirements: 3.14.2 (protect at designated locations), 3.14.4 (update the mechanisms), and 3.14.5 (periodic and real-time scans). Rev 3 collects all three into one requirement: 03.14.02. The image above shows where each Rev 2 objective lands. Objective 3.14.2[a], which identifies the designated locations, has no Rev 3 match.

Step 2: Take credit for previous work

Some Rev 2 assessment objectives don't directly satisfy Rev 3 assessment objectives, but some small adjustments will often get us there. The assessment language changed, but actions from a Rev 2 Huntress resource may still meet Rev 3 requirements.

In the 03.14.02 example above, you'll see that some of your Rev 2 efforts require fact-checking to see if they line up with the new language:

Rev 3 gets more specific about where malicious code protections must be implemented. If you identified designated locations for malware protection during your Rev 2 implementation and didn't cover all "system entry and exit points," you might have a gap.

Rev 3 also points to "configuration management policy and procedures" as the documents governing malware updates. If policies and procedures don't describe updating malicious code protections when new releases are available, you may have some edits to make.

The malware scanning objectives (3.14.5[a] through [c]) from Rev 2 should satisfy their Rev 3 counterparts. Take credit for work you've already completed!

Step 3: Apply the DoD ODPs

Some Revision 3 requirements provide blank values so an organization can define frequencies, time periods, and other parameters. After 800-171 Rev 3 was published, the Department of Defense published a set of their own parameters for contractors to use in nonfederal systems.

03.14.02 has one blank parameter: how often the malicious code protection mechanisms scan the system.

A value that is stricter than your current practice means a configuration change. In the case above, Managed Antivirus settings can supplement real-time protection with scheduled weekly scans. This frequency is already specified in the Huntress Baseline Configuration created to meet Revision 2 requirements.

Step 4: Attack the gaps

Rev 3 adds requirements and objectives with no Rev 2 equivalent. Backfill them last, once steps 1 through 3 show what is actually missing.

03.14.02 has one new item: configure the mechanisms to block, quarantine, or otherwise mitigate detected malicious code. While Huntress Managed EDR and Microsoft Defender work together to block malicious code, automatic host isolation could easily be one of your "other actions." Existing actions we already include in Huntress CMMC resources address this, and so the "gap" is really documenting how your Revision 2 implementation meets this new requirement.

How Huntress is handling the transition

Huntress has partnered with DEFCERT to chart an upgrade path to 800-171 Revision 3. This includes an updated Shared Responsibility Matrix, Operations Plan, SSP statements, and evidence. Since Revision 2 remains important for existing contracts, any new documentation will map back to Rev 2.

Learn more about how Huntress helps you achieve and maintain CMMC compliance.

Title: Detecting Timeroasting the Hard Way
Context: The important finding at this layer: the attacker-controlled fields from the packet, the RID at offset 48 and the flag byte at offset 53, flow through w32time only as a RID...
Full Text:
Most detection rules come from one of two places: a vendor feed or a breach report. There is a third source that stays underused, and it is the one that actually teaches you something. Read the protocol spec, then read the binary that implements it. Not the attacker's tool, and not the vendor's marketing page: the target's own code.

This post is what happened when I did that for timeroasting. The detection you can copy for it today is a volumetric counter of connections to UDP/123 that understands nothing about the protocol. Nobody keys on what actually separates an attacker from a member, and the extended form has no coverage at all. So I reversed the binary to understand the protocol well enough to detect it properly. This is the walk from the bytes in netlogon.dll to detection that works against a real fleet. Reversing the crypto that precisely also hands you a working cracker, which is a nice bonus, but detection is the point. That is the "hard way" in the title: there is no public documentation for the extended crypto and no hashcat module for it, so you recover both by reading the binary.

The roasts you know

There are three roasts most people can name without thinking.

Kerberoasting. Request a service ticket for any account with an SPN, then crack the encrypted ticket blob offline.

AS-REP roasting. For accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication turned off, grab the AS-REP and crack its encrypted chunk.

Timeroasting. Per Tom Tervoort's 2023 research, abuse Microsoft's proprietary NTP authentication extension, MS-SNTP, to make a DC hand you a password-derived MAC for any computer or trust account, with zero authentication, then crack it offline.

The form nobody cracks

Timeroasting's request comes in two authenticator formats, and only one of them has public cracking support: hashcat has a mode for the legacy form and none for the other.

MS-SNTP lets a domain client confirm that a time response really came from a DC that knows the client's machine password, without the client authenticating first. The client sends an NTP request that names an account by its Relative Identifier (RID), and the DC answers with a MAC computed over the response using that account's password-derived key. A RID is the tail of an account's Security Identifier (SID), its unique index within the domain; naming a target by that number is all "sweep RIDs" means. Sign for whatever RID I name, no auth required: that is the entire attack surface. Sweep RIDs, collect MACs, crack offline.

The form everyone knows is 68 bytes on the wire, and its MAC is built with MD5. That is what hashcat mode 31300 cracks, what timeroast.py and netexec produce, and what every writeup covers.

The form almost nobody covers is 120 bytes, and it is neither new nor exotic. Microsoft added it to the spec as the preferred option, explicitly because of weaknesses in MD5, and it has been in real traffic for years. chrony added handling for it back in 2016, and modern Windows w32time sends it by default, to the point that it broke time synchronization against Samba AD domain controllers (DCs), which do not implement the extended form. The documented workaround is a Windows registry flag, SignatureAuthAllowed=0, that forces clients back to the legacy authenticator. Its MAC is built with an SP800-108 key derivation step followed by HMAC-SHA512. The gap is this: the exact crypto is not documented anywhere I could find, and hashcat has no module for it, so when you collect the extended MAC the legacy cracker cannot touch it.

Note: The two forms are trivial to tell apart on the wire. A 68-byte authenticated NTP packet is the legacy form; a 120-byte one is the extended form. Keep them apart in your head, because which form you have decides whether your cracker works, though as we will see, building detection on size is a mistake.

Why a defender should care

Timeroasting leaves no authentication event. The targeted accounts never log on, so there are no 4768, 4769, 4624, or 4776 events. That part of the usual claim is true, and it is where the attack earns its reputation for being quiet.

But quiet is not invisible. The DC still receives and answers a burst of UDP/123, and that is visible on the wire and in host network telemetry if you collect it, the half of the story most writeups skip. The extended form adds one wrinkle: if your DC speaks the 120-byte dialect and your collection assumes 68-byte MD5, your cracker produces nothing, and you misread an account as safe because you cracked the wrong format.

So the defender's questions are simple. Can you see the request happen? And if you harvest the MAC, can you actually crack it? We will answer both, but first we have to know exactly what the DC computes, and for that we read its code.

The two forms on the wire

Both forms are a standard 48-byte NTP packet with an authenticator appended. Two fields carry the rest of this post:

The KeyIdentifier at offset 48 (the target RID, little-endian)

In the extended form, a Flags byte at offset 53 whose 0x01 bit means USE_OLDKEY_VERSION

The remaining extended fields are defined in [MS-SNTP] and sit at their defaults in a request.

A 68-byte authenticator is the legacy form (48-byte header, 4-byte KeyID, 16-byte MD5 MAC); a 120-byte authenticator is the extended form. The client sends the MAC zeroed, and the DC fills it in and echoes the structure back.

Reading the code instead of guessing

The spec tells you the shape. It says, roughly, "K equals KDF of the key, a label, and a context, and the checksum is HMAC-SHA512 of K over the message." That is not enough to write a cracker. What is the label, down to the byte? How is the RID turned into the context? Which hash drives the KDF? Guess any of these wrong and your cracker produces confident garbage.

So I did not guess. Everything below is read off the actual binaries from a live, fully patched Windows Server 2025 domain controller (build 26100.33438), in radare2. I pulled w32time.dll and netlogon.dll off the DC over SMB and read them there.

Step 1: the crypto is not where you would expect it

My first assumption was that the signing happened in w32time.dll, since that is the service listening on UDP/123. It does not. I grepped the binary for the KDF label and came up empty:

rabin2 -zzq w32time.dll | grep -i "sntp-ms" -> (nothing)

rabin2 -zzq w32time.dll | grep -iE "SP800|SHA512" -> (nothing)

What w32time does import tells the story. Its crypto is delegated to Netlogon through:

logoncli.dll: logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeServerSignature <- extended (SHA-512) logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeServerDigest <- legacy (MD5) logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeClientSignature logoncli.dll I_NetlogonComputeClientDigest logoncli.dll I_NetlogonGetTrustRid bcrypt.dll BCryptCreateHash / HashData / FinishHash / DestroyHash / GenRandom

So w32time parses the packet and dispatches. The "Signature" functions are the extended, SHA-512 path; the "Digest" functions are the legacy, MD5 path. The interesting bytes live in netlogon.dll.

Step 2: the w32time dispatch and the extended-vs-legacy branch

Figure 1: the time service imports I_NetlogonComputeServerSignature and I_NetlogonComputeServerDigest from logoncli.dll, and a string search for sntp-ms in w32time.dll comes back empty. The signing logic lives in Netlogon, not in w32time.

Two functions in w32time call both compute paths, and the server picks the SHA-512 path or the MD5 path based on the request it parsed. The important finding at this layer: the attacker-controlled fields from the packet, the RID at offset 48 and the flag byte at offset 53, flow through w32time only as a RID value and a key selector that get passed down to Netlogon. They are not used as a length, an index, or a buffer size anywhere in the parse.

Step 3: NlGetKDFKey, the function that builds the key

In netlogon.dll, the function that derives the KDF key uses its own debug-string name, NlGetKDFKey. It builds a BCryptKeyDerivation call with the SP800-108 counter-mode HMAC algorithm and three parameter buffers, and the disassembly (Figure 2) pins down the three things a cracker needs. The spec implies a KDF with "a label" and "a context." The bytes say: the PRF is HMAC-SHA512 (the hash-algorithm buffer is L"SHA512"), the label is the 8-byte "sntp-ms\0" with the null included (cbBuffer is 8 for a 7-character string), and the context is the 4-byte RID in little-endian, exactly as it arrived in the packet. Output is a fixed 64 bytes. Every size is constant, and nothing here is attacker-controlled.

Figure 2. radare2 disassembly of the buffer setup: the sntp-ms label and the L"SHA512" algorithm string being loaded into the BCryptKeyDerivation call that derives the signing key.

Step 4: NlComputeHMACMessageSignatureFromKey, the outer HMAC

The caller is NlComputeHMACMessageSignatureFromKey. It calls NlGetKDFKey, then HMACs the message under the derived key: the 64-byte derived key is the secret, the message is the fixed 48-byte NTP header, and the output is 64 bytes. Note the one place a caller-supplied length reaches anything: the input length to that hash call. It is used only as the number of bytes to hash, never as an allocation size or an index, and w32time hands Netlogon a fixed 48-byte NTP header for the message. Every other size is BCrypt-derived or the fixed 64. The function error-checks every allocation and every BCrypt call with its own labeled failure path.

The chain is now pinned: the NThash feeds a SHA-512 SP800-108 KDF keyed by the sntp-ms label and the RID, producing a 64-byte key, and that key HMACs the 48-byte NTP response. That is everything the detection needs to know about the crypto. The cracker also needs the exact byte layout, which I lay out next to the cracker below.

Proving it against a live DC

Reading bytes gives you a hypothesis; I wanted the DC to confirm it. First, reachability, because the extended form being in the spec does not mean a patched DC answers it. I probed a live computer-account RID with both forms and both key selectors. The result was reproducible five times out of five:

current key (flags=0) old key (flags=0x01) legacy (68B) 68-byte reply 68-byte reply extended (120B) silent timeout 120-byte reply (real HMAC-SHA512)

So the extended form is live on a fully patched DC, and it returns a genuine nonzero 64-byte checksum that changes every request, because the salt is the NTP response, which moves. The collector emits each old-key response as a single $sntp-ms-sha512$<RID>$<checksum>$<salt> line, the format laid out in full in the cracking section below. Because the salt is the live NTP response, no two captures are byte-identical, so the hash line in Figure 3 is one instance of that shape rather than a fixed value worth reprinting here.

Figure 3: The collector's three-way probe against the DC: a 68-byte legacy reply, an extended current-key request that times out, and an extended old-key 120-byte reply, with one sntp-ms-sha512 hash line produced.

Then the crypto proof: I wrote a small pure-Python reference (no dependencies) that implements the chain above, recovered the responding account's NT hash in the lab (the NT hash is just MD4 of the password, the long-term key every Windows account carries, and what both the MD5 and SHA-512 MACs are ultimately keyed on), and asked one question: does my code reproduce the DC's checksum from that hash? It does, exactly. The verifier reported the match and told me which parameters won, the 8-byte null-inclusive label and the little-endian RID context, confirmed against live output rather than assumed.

Figure 4. The reference implementation reproducing the DC's checksum from the account NT hash: the captured wire checksum equals the recomputed HMAC-SHA512, and the 8-byte label and little-endian RID context are confirmed, not assumed.

A reproducible known-answer test vector (synthetic, not a capture, so it corresponds to no figure) with a known password, safe to publish, so anyone reimplementing the KDF can check their work:

password : Summer2026! (example only, not a real account) NThash : 41aed72cec76816423703d8e545eea31 RID : 1104 (arbitrary; the RID is just KDF context) hash : $sntp-ms-sha512$1104$a24990178f8f309a190f08c9a8c5000ce126eef19b236b50cc680d592057cd1ec872d3de6b7fdc47d8a865cae2c5c277d8842f3d1a8b7b6bb0c06bbffebb6307$1c0400e90000000800000291564d5450000102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f101112131415161718191a1b1c1d1e1f

That current-key timeout deserves a note, because my first explanation for it was wrong. I had assumed it was specific to the DC's own never-rotated machine account. It is not. I retested across nine machine accounts, member computers included, and every one behaves the same way: legacy answers, extended old-key answers, extended current-key times out. So it is a property of this DC, not an artifact of one account. I do not have a confident explanation, and since modern Windows clients clearly use the extended form successfully in the wild, this DC's current-key behavior may not be representative, and I cannot rule out the simpler possibility that my collector's current-key request is itself malformed. Either way, I am flagging it as an open observation rather than resting any conclusion on it.

Cracking it: the bonus from reversing the KDF

Detecting the extended form never needed the KDF internals. But with the binary already open, getting the key derivation exactly right is a small extra step that hands you a working cracker.

Here is the construction, straight from the two functions above:

NThash = MD4(UTF-16LE(password)) # NTOWFv1, 16 bytes K = SP800-108-CounterMode( KI = NThash, PRF = HMAC-SHA512, Label = "sntp-ms\0" (8 bytes, includes the null), Context = RID (4 bytes, little-endian), L = 512 bits) # 64 bytes, one block checksum = HMAC-SHA512(K, NTP-response[0:48]) # 64 bytes

The SP800-108 fixed input, the way Microsoft's BCryptKeyDerivation assembles it (the same layout MS-GKDI uses, which is how I sanity-checked the counter and separator):

block(1) = HMAC-SHA512(NThash, BE32(1) || "sntp-ms\0" || 0x00 || LE32(RID) || BE32(512))

Four ways to get this wrong, every one of which silently breaks a cracker, and I would have shipped at least two if I had trusted the spec text alone:

The label is 8 bytes including the null, not the 7-byte sntp-ms you would type.

SP800-108 then inserts its own 0x00 separator after the label, so two null bytes land in the fixed input, not one.

The counter and length are big-endian 32-bit, but the RID context is little-endian 32-bit: mixed endianness inside one buffer.

It is a KDF and then an HMAC, two HMAC-SHA512 passes, not a single HMAC over the message.

Before the tooling, two questions I keep getting, because together they decide how much this should worry you.

Is the 120-byte form a different attack?

No. Same protocol and trigger (unauthenticated MS-SNTP, name an account by RID, collect a MAC, no auth), same targets (computer and trust accounts), same collection (sweep RIDs), same goal. Only the MAC construction changes. Legacy builds its MAC with MD5 over the NT hash and the response; extended builds it with an SP800-108 key derivation and then HMAC-SHA512. Same secret, same request, a different MAC on the wire.

Is it harder to crack?

Yes, in two senses, and only one of them is real cryptographically.

The first is per-guess cost, where it is genuinely harder. Legacy is one MD4 plus one MD5, and MD5 is about as GPU-friendly as a hash gets. Extended is one MD4 plus two HMAC-SHA512 passes (roughly eight SHA-512 compressions), nothing precomputable across guesses since the derived key depends on both the RID and the candidate, and SHA-512's 64-bit operations are deliberately GPU-unfriendly. So it is much slower per guess. I will not hand you a multiplier against Kerberoasting, because that depends on the ticket's encryption type (RC4, mode 13100, versus AES, mode 19700); benchmark it against hashcat's other SHA-512 HMAC modes on your own hardware.

The second is whether it protects a weak password, and there the answer is barely. Both forms key off the same NT hash, so a weak password falls to either and a random machine secret falls to neither; the MD5-versus-SHA-512 difference only changes the price per guess, not which accounts are roastable. Password entropy is the protection, exactly as it always was.

So why would an attacker reach for the extended form at all, when the 68-byte form is cheaper to crack and has a working hashcat mode? Two reasons, neither of which is that it is a better attack:

First, evasion: on a fleet where legitimate clients already send 120-byte requests, extended traffic blends into the baseline, while the 68-byte tools stick out.

Second, future-proofing, for a day when Microsoft disables the legacy MD5 path. The "your cracker silently fails" trap is real but narrow: it only catches a tool that requests the extended form and then formats the output as legacy. Whoever collects 120-byte responses can see they are 120 bytes.

Here is the current state of cracking:

What hashcat cracks today: the 68-byte legacy form, mode 31300, MD5.

What hashcat cracks for the extended form: nothing in a released build yet; there is no upstream module. Issue 3629, which produced 31300, is the MD5 one.

So if you collect the extended MAC today, your options are a custom kernel or a CPU reference implementation. I wrote the reference and used this hash format, matching the existing $sntp-ms$ convention:

$sntp-ms-sha512$<RID>$<checksum_hex>$<salt_hex>

...where the salt is the 48-byte NTP response. For comparison, the legacy form captured off the same DC (hashcat 31300):

1000:$sntp-ms$f3c43f1f39a61012e634983008213633$1c0400e90000000c000002a6564d5450ee667af63d863d9cee66797600000000ee667b146da6b866ee667b146da72a7b

Building the hashcat module

Since the reference proves the algorithm, the next step is a real hashcat module, so the extended form is as cheap to attack, and therefore as urgent to detect, as the legacy one. The module below is written and passes hashcat's own self-test on a GPU. The algorithm is DC-verified through the Python reference, and the module plus its OpenCL kernel clear tools/test.py -m 31350 cleanly across the single and multi vectors at vector widths 1 and 4, and crack a known-password vector end to end. On an Apple M3 Pro the mode benchmarks at 17.6 MH/s (hashcat -b -m 31350).

31350 is not a released hashcat mode number. It is a placeholder; the maintainers assign the real one when this goes upstream, so you build it from the source below. Getting the kernel to pass took fixing exactly the byte-level traps this post keeps warning about: the SP800-108 L value has to land as the big-endian bytes 00 00 02 00 at the right offset in the KDF message, not as a little-endian word, and the password has to be decoded as real UTF-16LE. Guess either wrong and the self-test fails the same way, the same lesson as the label and the context.

The self-test oracle that hashcat's tools/test.py uses to make a known hash (tools/test_modules/m31350.py) is the clearest statement of the whole algorithm in a few lines:

LABEL = b"sntp-ms\x00" # 8 bytes, trailing null INCLUDED def _nthash(word): return _md4(utf16le(word, "utf-8")) # NTOWFv1 = MD4(UTF-16LE(pw)) def _kdf(nt_hash, rid): # SP800-108 CTR, PRF HMAC-SHA512, single block (L=512) fixed = struct.pack(">I", 1) + LABEL + b"\x00" + struct.pack("<I", rid) + struct.pack(">I", 512) # BE32(counter=1) label 0x00 sep LE32(RID) BE32(L=512) <- the byte trap return hmac.new(nt_hash, fixed, hashlib.sha512).digest() def _hash(word, salt_bin, rid): # checksum = HMAC-SHA512(K, 48-byte NTP response) k = _kdf(_nthash(word), rid) checksum = hmac.new(k, salt_bin, hashlib.sha512).digest() return "sntp-ms-sha512%d%s%s" % (rid, checksum.hex(), salt_bin.hex())

The full hashcat module (module_31350.c, the OpenCL kernel m31350-pure.cl, and the m31350.py self-test oracle) ships alongside this post. Drop the three into a hashcat source tree and build; the only thing that matters before any pull request is the self-test passing:

make -j && tools/test.py -m 31350

Watching it recover a password

A module is only interesting if it recovers something. Here it is against a collected extended MAC: the dependency-free reference cracker first, then the same recovery in hashcat.

Figure 5. Recovering a weak machine-account password from a collected extended (SHA-512) timeroast MAC with the pure-Python reference cracker. The crack is entirely offline, no DC contact and no lockout. A pre-created account still on its lowercase-name default falls instantly; a normal random machine secret would not fall to any wordlist.

Figure 6. The same recovery in hashcat with the new mode 31350.

The extended form now cracks with the same tooling as the legacy one, built from the module in this post. This run is on a Kali box against a six-word list, so it finishes before hashcat can measure a representative rate; that box benchmarks at about 339 kH/s (hashcat -b), while the 17.6 MH/s above is the M3 Pro GPU.

The extended form stops being a research curiosity and becomes exactly as cheap to crack as the legacy one, which only matters for accounts whose password is guessable in the first place. So the next question is who that actually is.

Who is actually at risk

All of that, the reference implementation, the hash format, the module, is about turning a collected MAC into a password. But it assumes you have something worth cracking, and that set is narrower than a sweep's raw length suggests. Run one and look at what actually answers:

Figure 7. A NetExec timeroast sweep against the lab DC. RID 1000 and the 1166-1195 cluster answer; the 1001-1165 gaps stay silent. Every line is the 68-byte legacy form, because NetExec emits only legacy.

The gaps are the finding. In that sweep, RID 1000 answers, then nothing until 1166, then a cluster through 1195. The missing RIDs, 1001-1165, and the holes inside the 11xx block, are not users the sweep skipped. They are users the DC refused to sign for. You are not looking at a filtered list of the domain; you are looking at the complete set of accounts the DC was willing to answer for, and that set is computer and trust accounts only.

Why? the DC produces a MAC only when the named RID resolves to an account that carries a machine secret, meaning a computer or trust account. A normal user account returns an error and w32time simply does not reply. No reply, no MAC, nothing for the tool to print. RID 1000 answered, so it is a machine or trust account; fire a request straight at user RID 1110 (tony.soprano) in that gap and the DC stays silent.

Concretely: timeroasting reaches computer and trust accounts, full stop. That is why the crackable population is the narrow set worth naming: image-built or never-rotated machines, hand-set trusts, non-Windows joins. It is also why targeted timeroasting has to exist: to roast a real user, an attacker with domain admin first flips that user into a machine-looking account, appending a $ to its name and setting its userAccountControl to a workstation trust so the DC will sign for it, then reverts. Without that rename, a user's RID in this sweep returns nothing. The gaps are your users. The rename needs domain admin and is loud, so it is a different risk class from the unauthenticated sweep this post is about.

Can defenders even see this?

The targeted accounts never authenticate, so this never reaches identity analytics. But the request is still a packet on the wire and a connection on a host, and both are collectable. Three sources see it:

The DC's own Windows Filtering Platform audit (event 5156) logs w32time accepting the UDP/123 connection, when that subcategory is enabled.

Host EDR sees the network connection, and there is already a public Sentinel detection that counts UDP/123 connections per source over DeviceNetworkEvents.

On the attacker's own machine, any process that is not the time service sending UDP/123 to a DC is a high-signal EDR hit.

So the problem is not that nobody can see it; it is that nobody is looking at the right telemetry, because everyone reaches for authentication logs first.

One product acknowledges timeroasting at all, Microsoft Defender for Identity, and it only catches the loud privileged variant: the sAMAccountName rename of the targeted attack, not the unauthenticated sweep this post is about. I take that alert apart in detail later; the point here is that naming a technique is not detecting it.

The harder question is what the good signal is, and here the extended form changes the answer.

Do not build on packet size. On an older fleet a 120-byte authenticated request looked rare. On a modern one it is the reverse: Windows clients send the extended form as normal time sync, and it is the 68-byte request that stands out, because both public timeroast tools emit only 68 bytes. Either way, size is a baseline question, not an attack signal, and which size is the odd one out depends on your Windows versions.

The signal that holds, for both sizes and even for a single packet, is simple: a legitimate member only ever asks the DC to sign for its own machine account. Resolve the source IP to a computer account (via DHCP or DNS) and then to its RID, and a request for any other RID is anomalous on its face. That catches a slow, one-RID-at-a-time sweep that no volume threshold would, and it does not care whether the packet is 68 or 120 bytes.

Volume is the fallback. A single source asking a DC to sign for many different RIDs in a short window is a sweep. It is weaker than the own-RID check, because a patient attacker can pace under the threshold, but it needs no IP-to-RID mapping, so it is the easy first rule.

Writing the detection, and the bug that ate all four of my rules

I wrote four Suricata rules and then did the thing I have learned to always do: I ran them through the actual engine instead of trusting that they looked right. Suricata 8.0.7, against a real capture of a sweep: 41 legacy requests and 41 extended requests from one host to a DC.

The engine immediately caught a mistake I would have shipped. I had left C-style /* ... */ comments inside the rule bodies to annotate them. Suricata has no inline comment syntax, so every rule that contained one failed to load, and the engine told me plainly that zero rules were loaded. Strip the comments.

With that fixed, all four loaded clean and fired. The extended-request rule matched all 41 extended packets and, because it is rate-limited to one alert per source per five minutes, logged a single alert, which is working as designed. The old-key rule matched and logged all 41 old-key requests. The legacy sweep rule fired once, at the 25th distinct RID, exactly where its threshold says it should. The extended sweep rule did the same on the extended packets. The fast.log evidence:

[1:5200003:1] MS-SNTP authenticated-NTP RID sweep (Timeroast) {UDP} 10.x.x.x:42198 -> 10.x.x.x:123 [1:5200001:1] MS-SNTP ExtendedAuthenticator request (possible extended Timeroast) {UDP} ... [1:5200002:1] MS-SNTP ExtendedAuthenticator USE_OLDKEY_VERSION (extended Timeroast, old key) {UDP} ... (x41) [1:5200004:1] MS-SNTP extended RID sweep (Timeroast) {UDP} ...

That first pass validated the mechanics and taught me the /* */ lesson, but all four rules were pinned to packet size, and the evidence that modern Windows sends the extended form means most of them do not survive a real fleet. Here is what I would actually ship. Set your own $DC_SERVERS.

Start with the volumetric sweep, deliberately size-agnostic so it catches both forms. An authenticated MS-SNTP request to a DC is 68 or 120 bytes; a plain NTP client request is 48, so dsize above 56 selects the authenticated ones, and the byte_test on the low three bits of byte 0 keeps it to client-mode (mode 3) requests, not a mode-4 server reply that happens to be large:

alert udp any any -> $DC_SERVERS 123 (msg:"MS-SNTP authenticated-NTP sweep to DC (Timeroast, either form)"; dsize:>56; byte_test:1,=,3,0,bitmask 0x07; threshold:type threshold, track by_src, count 25, seconds 60; classtype:attempted-recon; sid:5200010; rev:1;)

Keep the old-key flag, but as a hypothesis to test rather than a verdict:

alert udp any any -> $DC_SERVERS 123 (msg:"MS-SNTP ExtendedAuthenticator USE_OLDKEY_VERSION"; dsize:120; content:"|01|"; offset:53; depth:1; classtype:attempted-recon; sid:5200002; rev:1;)

The spec ties that flag to a client-side Key Selector, and clients validate responses against both the current and the previous password, so a legitimate client around a machine-password rotation could plausibly set it. I have not seen a real member do it, but I have not watched enough real extended traffic to rule it out, so capture your own fleet's requests and look. If none of your members ever set the flag, this is your best size-based signal; if some do, demote it.

Both rules load clean and fire in Suricata 8.0.7 on a captured sweep (the volumetric one three times as the threshold rolls, the old-key one once per matching packet) and stay silent on a plain client.

Figure 8. The two rules I would ship, in Suricata 8.0.7 against a captured sweep: both load clean, the old-key rule (5200002) fires on all 41 old-key requests, and the volumetric rule (5200010) fires 3 times as its threshold rolls.

Do not ship a rule that simply alerts on a 120-byte request. On a modern fleet that fires on every Windows member doing normal time sync. It is a baseline measurement, not an attack signal.

The durable detector is not a Suricata rule at all, because the question that separates attacker from member (is this RID the sender's own?) needs an IP-to-account mapping Suricata does not have. Do it in Zeek or your SIEM: for each authenticated NTP request to a DC, pull the RID from offset 48, resolve the source IP to a computer account (DHCP or DNS, then LDAP to its objectSid and RID), and alert when the requested RID is not the source's own. That catches a single packet, a slow sweep, and both forms, and it does not depend on which size your fleet treats as normal.

Here is that check as a skeleton. The comparison is trivial; the work is the enrichment, a source-IP-to-own-RID table refreshed out of band from DHCP or DNS plus an LDAP lookup of each host's objectSid.

# For each authenticated MS-SNTP request to a DC: on UDP packet to DC:123 where len(payload) in {68, 120} # 48 = plain NTP, ignore and (payload[0] & 0x07) == 3: # client mode 3, not a server reply requested_rid = le32(payload[48:52]) # KeyIdentifier, little-endian own_rid = ip_to_rid[src_ip] # enrichment: DHCP/DNS -> LDAP objectSid -> RID if own_rid is None: alert("authenticated MS-SNTP from a host with no RID mapping") # triage, not a verdict elif requested_rid != own_rid: alert("host asked the DC to sign for a RID that is not its own") # the durable signal

One honest caveat on wiring this to Zeek: the stock ntp_message event parses standard NTP and never surfaces the MS-SNTP KeyIdentifier, so you reach offset 48 with a small Spicy analyzer or raw-payload access, not three lines of script. Getting the RID off the wire and keeping the IP-to-RID table fresh is the real work; the mismatch test is the easy part.

Where these rules will lie to you

Measure your own 68-versus-120 baseline before you alert on either size, treat the volumetric rule as the weak first pass that a paced attacker or a NAT'd source can fool and the own-RID check as the one that holds, and baseline the old-key flag before you trust it.

Fingerprinting the tools, and the rule not to write

I ran the two public timeroast tools against a DC in the lab, SecuraBV's timeroast.py and timeroast-ng, and diffed their packets against a real NTP client byte for byte, to see whether there is a tool fingerprint worth keying on. There is, with one trap.

The trap first, because it is the tempting rule and it is wrong. Do not alert on a zero 16-byte MAC in [truncated for CSV - full text is in the JSON export]

Title: RMM Alerts at 2 AM: An MSP and SOC Incident Response Story
Context: Once Huntress confirmed the attacker still had access, TruePath locked down the client's environment again and finished the cleanup it had started after the first incident
Full Text:
Cybercriminals don't check the clock before they go hunting for gaps. In early September, a 2am alert in the Huntress Security Operations Center (SOC) flagged suspicious remote monitoring and management (RMM) activity. It was in the client network of a managed service provider (MSP), TruePath IT, and close to 1,000 endpoints were at risk. Twelve days later, the alert queue lit up again, indicating that the attacker still had access to the environment. These two incidents cost the client an estimated $3 million in downtime and a lot of stress.

Learn how TruePath IT worked with Huntress to contain two rogue ScreenConnect deployments in less than two weeks, and how recovery plans shifted after the second incident was discovered.

One account, nearly 1,000 "doors"

In the initial incident, the attackers compromised an account with wide-reaching admin rights and used it to push out rogue ScreenConnect instances.

Figure 1: Huntress internal communication to communicate with the partner and contain the incident

ScreenConnect lets a technician take over a machine remotely to fix a problem, run scripts, and push updates. That's a great setup when it's your technician and a bad one when it's an attacker. This one put nearly 1,000 "doors" within reach of an unwanted intruder, and TruePath was responsible for the building.

The Huntress SOC runs 24/7, so they isolated the affected endpoints and sent a critical incident report right away.

Figure 2: Critical incident report from the Huntress SOC explaining the first rogue RMM incident

Why TruePath IT asked for the SOC phone call anyway

Tom Warren, Vice President of Operations at TruePath IT, stepped in just before 5am, to pick up where TruePath's CEO left off in handling the incident overnight. He had the incident report in hand, but asked for a phone call with the SOC anyway. The client would treat whatever he said next as final, so he wanted SOC support to talk through this specific incident and the impact of each decision.

Figure 3: How partners and customers can request SOC support

A SOC analyst was on a call in under 10 minutes, then joined a call with the client's IT director and stayed until the team felt ready to act. With the client's executive team closely watching the disruption, the IT director had solid, confirmed facts to carry up the chain as the incident response unfolded.

The pressure to reopen without enough cleanup

By the time the first wave of malicious activity had settled, the client had been down for about two days, and leadership wanted to know when business operations would return to normal.

Rushing recovery on a compromised network is risky, often causing more damage. TruePath had a priority-user list ready and released machines in targeted batches. Under pressure from leadership, though, the client's team put some endpoints that were still compromised back into use before they were fully cleaned up.

Groundhog Day, Rogue ScreenConnect Edition

A second rogue ScreenConnect instance showed up in the same environment 12 days later, this time delivering what looked like a ransomware executable. The attacker had kept their foothold on endpoints that went back into production before they were ready.

Once Huntress confirmed the attacker still had access, TruePath locked down the client's environment again and finished the cleanup it had started after the first incident.

That meant telling the client's CEO, who had just spent days recovering, that systems were going offline again. Logistics deadlines were slipping, and nobody could use their machines to qualify orders.

Trust, but Verify, One Endpoint at a Time

After the second lockdown, nothing returned to production until the client's IT team verified remediation work for each affected endpoint and an executive gave verbal approval. The lesson learned was that there has to be clear evidence of recovery before going back into production mode. The reopening was slower, but the client never had to read a ransomware note.

Pre-Game Your Next 2 am Alert

These conversations are much easier to have before an incident than during one. Whether you run IT for your own company or manage it for clients, answer these questions ahead of time:

If an active threat shows up, who's authorized to isolate the affected systems?

Who makes the decisions, and can your IT or security team act right away, or does someone need to sign off first?

Who communicates with leadership during an incident?

How much downtime can the business tolerate?

How quickly could you recover? Having backups doesn't automatically mean you can restore operations quickly.

A few technical habits also shrink the room an attacker has to work with:

Decide which remote access tools belong in your environment and block everything else by default.

Watch what normally runs in your environment before you enforce anything, then clean up what shouldn't be there, like leftover software from a previous IT provider, a project, or a trial that never moved forward.

Look at your network from the outside. Find which ports and services are exposed to the internet, and decide which need tighter protection, such as a hardened firewall policy.

Watch the full livestream, "Inside the Incident: What Happens When Our SOC Calls", to learn what good SOC support at 2am looks like.

Title: What Business Email Compromise (BEC) Looks Like & How to Catch It
Context: 6% of Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) signals so far in 2026, according to the Huntress Tragic Quadrant, our ranking of the top attacker techniques by impact
Full Text:
If you're looking for a history lesson on your company's finances, start in your inbox, where you might find invoices and vendor details, along with the renewal haggling that shows exactly what you pay and to whom.

Cybercriminals can be history buffs too. Digging through old email threads shows them exactly who to impersonate and how money actually moves. In 2025 alone, the FBI logged more than $20.8 billion in cybercrime losses, with roughly $3 billion tied to business email compromise (BEC), second only to investment fraud.

Business email compromise (BEC) pays because it hides in the long-running vendor and billing conversations you already trust.

"I'd notice if someone was in my inbox"

You might assume you know the signs of an intruder lurking in your mailbox. We've all been trained to recognize the obvious, sloppy signs of phishing.

BEC is stealthier. Often with the help of AI, attackers aim at specific targets by crafting legit-looking phishing and social engineering scams to steal credentials or session tokens for access and persistence. They set up inbox rules that quietly move messages into folders nobody checks, hiding their dirty work in plain sight. This gives them time to figure out how to route money to their own accounts straight from your mailbox.

Here's how that attack chain plays out in a real Microsoft tenant. Huntress CEO Kyle Hanslovan breaks down how attackers sneak into Microsoft 365 mailboxes with low-fi resources to stage attacks like BEC.

What the data says

According to the FBI, reported BEC losses have climbed more than tenfold since 2015.

Figure 1: Reported BEC losses by year. Source: FBI IC3 annual reports, 2015 to 2024.

The Huntress 2026 Cyber Threat Report puts numbers behind the identity tradecraft that fuels BEC:

Logins with a shady footprint made up 37% of the identity threats we tracked, often as the first step toward email compromise and wire fraud.

Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks, which steal a session token and let the attacker skip the password and the MFA prompt, accounted for 18.9% of identity-based threats in 2025.

Mailbox manipulation and persistence, a key BEC technique, accounts for 24.6% of Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) signals so far in 2026, according to the Huntress Tragic Quadrant, our ranking of the top attacker techniques by impact.

How one gut check stopped a BEC attempt

Latisha Edwards, Accounts Receivable Specialist on the Huntress billing team, received an email that looked like just every other order or renewal message in the queue. It referenced a real partner account with an order form that looked like the right next step.

But something felt off. The order form had a "log in" link embedded in it, which didn't match how this partner usually handled business. Instead of clicking, Latisha emailed her contact at the partner to follow up. That follow-up confirmed the email was a BEC attempt, sent by someone impersonating the partner. Stopping this attack came down to one person slowing down long enough to ask a question. The email looked right because it sat inside a conversation the team already trusted.

Figure 2: A real-world BEC email attempt caught by the Huntress billing team

What you can do to slow down BEC

Now that you've seen what BEC looks like in the wild, let's dig into what you can do about it.

Encouraging your teammates to ask questions is the first step in a good defense against BEC. The Huntress billing team caught this one because Latisha felt safe asking about it.

From there, build good mailbox hygiene habits. The attack can start in your mailbox or arrive as an email from someone posing as a partner, and each one calls for a different kind of check.

For your own mailboxes, watch for inbox rules that don't seem to make sense. Set up alerts for any new forwarding rule, especially one that sends mail to an external domain.

Figure 3: Hidden inbox rules in a 2026 token replay campaign.

For emails that appear to come from partners, flag any request to change account numbers or payment instructions, or any unexpected link that asks you to log in, as high risk, and check the sender's actual address. Verify it directly with your usual contact through a channel you already trust, like a known phone number or portal.

What technology can do to shut down BEC

BEC scams are built to slip right past you. Here's where Huntress fills the gaps.

Managed Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) watches for identity-driven threat behavior across Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace, including session hijacking, suspicious logins, and malicious inbox and forwarding rules, backed by our 24/7 human-led, AI-centric Security Operations Center (SOC).

Managed Identity Security Posture Management (ISPM) works earlier in the attack chain, closing the misconfigurations and policy drift that let attackers into mailboxes and helping enforce conditional access policies.

Managed Security Awareness Training (SAT) helps your people recognize when to pause and verify a change to a payment.

Figure 3: Example of BEC activity flagged by ITDR

The most dangerous BEC email looks exactly like the one you were expecting. Start defending your identities against BEC today with a free trial of Huntress Managed ITDR.

Title: CVE-2026-84869 in ScreenConnect Exploited to Run Malicious Files on MSP Technician Accounts
Context: The malware, called SCKit, appears to be leveraging a vulnerable third-party extension on the server side of ScreenConnect and not directly exploiting CVE-2026-84869, but...
Full Text:
What Is CVE-2026-84869?

ConnectWise disclosed CVE-2026-84869 on September 8, 2026, with a CVSS score of 9.9, and CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on September 11. ConnectWise's advisory stated that in both Support and Access sessions, a guest could trigger file-transfer actions that the technician's host client processed without authorization or confirmation, including running the file with elevated rights. ConnectWise listed 26.6.5 as the fixed version for host clients and Access agents, and recommended removing the TransferFiles permission as an interim mitigation.

Figure 1: CVE-2026-84869 file transfer spray campaign by the numbers

In the days leading up to CVE-2026-84869's disclosure, Huntress stood up a Rapid Response to worm-like activity that spawned rogue ScreenConnect clients and dropped malicious VBScript files across several customer environments. On November 11, we stood up another Rapid Response to more worm-like activity where an attacker used Run commands on cloud-hosted panels to install rogue ScreenConnect clients and session-cookie relays on hundreds of managed endpoints. The malware, called SCKit, appears to be leveraging a vulnerable third-party extension on the server side of ScreenConnect and not directly exploiting CVE-2026-84869, but attempting to stage it as a "relay trap" for subsequent technician connections.

This most recent activity is distinct from a separate campaign we reported on November 13 that planted unauthorized guest sessions disguised with crypto exchange names on more than 100 MSP ScreenConnect servers. While we did not observe the attacker using the unauthorized sessions in this manner, the crypto exchange names may be intended to lure a technician into opening the session and running a malicious file on their client.

An MSP technician's workstation typically holds RMM consoles, saved credentials, and access to every customer, making it an exceptionally attractive target. When a technician joins a remote session, their ScreenConnect host client and the guest machine can exchange files. Normally, the technician decides what moves and what runs.

A malicious guest exploiting CVE-2026-84869 can push a file to the technician's machine and get the technician's own client to run it. From the technician's view, no prompt appears. They only have to join the session, whether from an attacker-controlled machine or a real customer's support session that the attacker has slipped into as an extra guest.

Huntress Observations

A full compromise in 9 seconds

On November 12, we observed a technician at one MSP using their ScreenConnect host client to join a blank-named Access session on the MSP's server. Here's what the process telemetry from the technician's workstation shows, in UTC:

Figure 2: The CVE-2026-84869 exploitation chain on a technician workstation on November 12, 2026

The attacker now has their own remote-access client on the technician's machine that looks like legitimate ScreenConnect and named after Windows Update.

The observed curl commands suggest that the attacker may have expected unreliable networks in their spraying attempts:

-A "Mozilla/5.0" --ssl-no-revoke --tlsv1.2 -f -L -C - --connect-timeout 20 --max-time 900 --retry 2 --speed-limit 2048 --speed-time 60

The spray: hundreds of thousands of requests, waiting for someone to join

How did that batch file reach the technician? On other MSPs' servers, we can see the delivery side in the server's own database.

Across 42 MSP ScreenConnect servers between October 20 and November 16, attacker guests made 688,000 "run file" requests for files named update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat from 29 source IP addresses. On the busiest server, 10 guest sessions from seven IPs made 70,414 requests over three weeks. The guests made repeated requests in case a technician happened to join.

Figure 3: Guest "run file" requests for update.bat-style batch files per ScreenConnect server, anonymized

The <8 hex> part of the file name looks like a payload or wave ID, not a per-victim ID. That's what ties the spray to the full compromise above: the exact file update_224ac089.bat was sprayed at five MSP ScreenConnect servers, starting within 2 seconds of each other at 16:03 UTC on November 12, 43 minutes before the compromise. Each server received it between 585 and 5,671 times, and three were still receiving it on November 16. The day before, the same sessions sprayed an earlier wave, update_c99a4b29.bat. We assess with high confidence that the spray operator and the masterdarky[.]com operator are the same.

What the spray guests look like:

blank session names or default-looking Windows hostnames

a claimed guest client version matching the server's own build (25.8.3.9466 on the busiest server)

no preview image, or a JPEG

an empty guest public key on about half of the sessions on the busiest server

All five sessions that sprayed update_224ac089.bat , and 27 spray sessions across 17 servers in total, have the session's Company property (CustomProperty1) set to crypto client. This is distinct from our previous reporting on crypto-exchange named decoys, which had this property left blank.

Canary song: A test run on a second technician

On November 13 at 01:49 UTC, a technician at another MSP joined a session presenting as a laptop. The guest, at 91.224.92[.]167, had been reconnecting to the MSP's server since late October, even after a technician queued it for uninstall. Two seconds after the technician joined, the guest pushed marker.txt. About three seconds after that, the technician's client ran it, and it opened in Notepad++. Nothing else followed until the host went offline 18 minutes later.

A harmless text file that announces itself is a classic canary; it proves the exploit works against this target before anything real is sent. The same IP pushed marker.txt three times at a technician at a third MSP in late October, each time while that technician was connected. We don't know whether that client ran it. Unlike the spray, this guest looked like a real, named Windows machine with a non-empty key and screenshot, which would fit a person driving it by hand.

This technician had also joined one of the unauthorized crypto-named guest sessions we were investigating about a minute earlier. While nothing came from that session, we mention it because it shows how close the two campaigns come in practice, targeting the same technician on the same vulnerable client inside a minute.

Path traversal into a technician's Startup folder

The most targeted activity we found happened in October, on one MSP's server. In three real support sessions technicians created for customers over multiple days, an attacker joined as an additional guest and asked the technician's client to run the following file:

../../../AppData/Roaming/Microsoft/Windows/STARTM~1/Programs/Startup/Sync.bat

If the client honored that path, it would drop a script into the technician's own Startup folder, where it would run at their next logon. Each push was sent while a different technician was connected (October 23, 24 and 27), from 193.26.115[.]63 and 57.128.131[.]66. Two of the technicians were on vulnerable Windows clients while the third used the Mac client, where a Windows Startup path failed.

A near-miss

On October 19, a guest at 91.224.92[.]83 (the same /24 as the canary IP) pushed Run-Lateral.bat seven times at a technician on a vulnerable 24.2 client. The closest push arrived 4.3 seconds after the technician disconnected, so nothing was delivered. We count this as a near-miss, not an exposure.

On another server, a guest at 107.148.223[.]37 pushed svc_payload.cmd 207 times; the technician joined only after the last push.

Figure 4: Spray activity per server and technician-exposure events, October 19 to November 16, 2026

What should MSPs do?

1. Patch technician clients now

Update every technician's ScreenConnect host client to 26.6.5 or later, and any Access agents ConnectWise lists. Updating the server alone doesn't fix this, because the vulnerable code runs on the technician's machine. Your server's connection history records which client version each technician used. In the cases discussed in this post, many technicians were still on 22.x, 24.2 and 25.8 clients weeks after the fix shipped.

If you can't patch today, remove the TransferFiles permission from roles and session groups, as ConnectWise advises.

2. Hunt for exposure

On the server (App_Data\Session.db, work on a copy), look for RanFiles (EventType 85) or SentFiles (86) events sent by a guest connection (ProcessType = 2), especially:

repeated requests for update.bat / update_<8hex>.bat in blank-named sessions

marker.txt, Run-Lateral.bat, svc_payload.cmd

any path containing ../

Then check whether a Host connection (ProcessType = 1) was open at that moment. That overlap is the exposure.

On technician workstations, look for:

ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe (or your branded client) running .bat, .cmd, .ps1, .vbs,.js, or .txt files from Documents\*\Temp\

anything in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\ you didn't put there, especially Sync.bat

folders named %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<8hex> and files named %TEMP%\wupdate_<8hex>.msi

WindowsUpdate.WindowsClient.exe or any ScreenConnect client whose command line points at a relay that isn't yours.

Kill spray sessions by deleting blank-named guest sessions that keep asking to run update*.bat. They come back, so check again.

3. If you find a hit

Isolate the technician's workstation, then:

Kill the rogue client and remove %LOCALAPPDATA%\wclient_<id> and the wupdate_<id>.msi.

Set seclogon back to its normal start type.

Rotate every credential that was reachable from that workstation: RMM, PSA, ScreenConnect, password vault, and customer admin accounts.

Assume the attacker could see everything the technician could.

4. Shrink the attack surface

Restrict who can join sessions as a guest, and review guest-side permissions on Support sessions.

Restrict access to your ScreenConnect web interface and installer downloads by IP or VPN where you can.

Don't join unattended sessions you can't tie to a customer.

Detection opportunities

Process: Parent ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe → child cmd.exe / powershell.exe / wscript.exe / notepad*.exe, where the command line references \ScreenConnect\Temp\ or \<brand>\Temp\ and the parent's arguments contain RunFile.

Process: msiexec.exe /a with TARGETDIR=%LOCALAPPDATA%\<prefix>_<8hex>, followed by runas /trustlevel:0x20000.

Process: curl downloading an .msi from a script that a ScreenConnect host client started.

Server: Guest-originated RanFiles with ../ traversal or a Startup path; high-volume RanFiles from one guest session.

Network: Outbound ScreenConnect relay connections (often port 8041) on domains you don't own.
